newsitem.title: USA: Rifkin turns down studio job at Sony.
newsitem.headline: Rifkin turns down studio job at Sony.

text.p: Arnold Rifkin, a top Hollywood talent agent, turned down an offer to head up Sony Corp's film studio Friday, leaving the troubled entertainment division to look for another candidate to replace studio boss Mark Canton.

In a brief statement, William Morris Agency said Rifkin, head of the agency's motion picture department, signed a "precedent-setting, long term agreement" with the firm, effectively taking him out of contention for any studio job.
"He is not a potential studio chief anymore," a spokesman for the agency said.
Terms of Rifkin's deal with William Morris were not disclosed.

Rifkin had been in talks with Sony this week about the studio job but negotiations broke down after Sony President Nobuyuki Idei decided to postpone naming a new studio chief until he determined the management structure for the entertainment division.

Some Hollywood insiders have suggested Sony Pictures President Alan Levine's job may also be in jeopardy but so far Idei has supported Levine in public, choosing to back his decision to force Canton out.
"I think Alan got half of what he wanted," said one industry source, referring to the decision to remove Canton but hold off hiring Rifkin.
In a statement issued late Friday, Levine did not name a replacement for Canton.

"I will now look to our motion picture executive group under the leadership of Columbia TriStar Vice Chair Lucy Fisher, working together with Columbia TriStar President Fred Bernstein, to strengthen its performance," Levine said. "I have confidence in this team's ability to maximize the performance of our strong slate of upcoming films."
Canton was not available to comment, but in a statement he said he was proud of his accomplishments at Sony.
"I gave my heart to the company, and I leave with the deepest affection and respect for its motion picture executives and appreciation for their support," he said.
Canton's departure is the latest in a series of high-level resignations at the studio, which Sony purchased in 1989 for $3.4 billion.

Earlier this summer, TriStar Pictures President Marc Platt left to take a job at MCA Inc's Universal Pictures and Columbia Pictures President Lisa Henson stepped down to form her own production company. In addition, Sid Ganis, the head of Sony Pictures marketing unit, also stepped down.

Industry analysts say Jeff Sagansky, executive vice president of Sony Corp of America, could be the next executive to leave after being passed over for the studio job. A former executive at CBS, Sagansky had reportedly lobbied for more responsibility at the entertainment division.
Canton, who joined Sony Pictures five years ago, came under fire this summer after several Sony films did poorly at the box office, including "The Fan", "The Cable Guy" and "Multiplicity".
"The Cable Guy" was a particularly embarrassing film for Sony because the studio had paid comedian Jim Carrey $20 million to star in the film and the studio spent millions more to promote it.
Terms of Canton's settlement with Sony were not disclosed, but industry sources said Canton probably received less than $10 million.

The management turmoil at Sony Pictures has captivated Hollywood, with many insiders predicting the Japanese electronics giant may ultimately decide to sell the studio. However, Sony officials insist the company has no plans to leave Hollywood.

Industry analysts said Rifkin, who heads up the motion picture department at William Morris, would have been a boost for Sony because of his links with the Hollywood community. His clients include Whoppi Goldberg, Bruce Willis and Sylvester Stallone.
